description: Tactic-organised MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise catalog used by /api/v1/mitre/coverage. The 14 tactics define stable matrix columns (Kibana convention). Techniques listed under each tactic are those the STRIX pipeline observes — sourced from RL_agent/synthetic/data_loader.py:TECHNIQUE_MAPPING + apps/api/docs/mitre_to_ckc.json. Sub-techniques (e.g. T1059.004) are intentionally omitted; the service rolls them up to their parent at query time, matching MitreMapper.technique() in apps/api/src/strix_api/core/mitre.py.

tactics.name: Reconnaissance
tactics.description: The adversary is gathering information about the target — network topology, employees, exposed services — to plan future operations. Activity here is often passive and external; CKC stage 1.

techniques.name: Active Scanning
techniques.description: Probing victim infrastructure (port scans, vulnerability scans, web-app sweeps) to enumerate exposed services and find weaknesses before initial access.

techniques.name: Brute Force
techniques.description: Iteratively guessing credentials when no valid pair is known. Includes password guessing, password spraying, and credential stuffing against authentication services.

tactics.name: Resource Development
tactics.description: Adversary stands up infrastructure they'll use later — domains, accounts, capabilities (malware, exploits, certs). Often invisible to the victim; not normally observed in lab telemetry.

tactics.name: Initial Access
tactics.description: First foothold inside the target environment. Phishing, exploit of an internet-facing app, or use of valid credentials are the dominant entry vectors.

techniques.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
techniques.description: Abusing a vulnerability in an internet-exposed service (web app, VPN, RDP gateway, etc.) to gain code execution on the host running it.

techniques.name: Valid Accounts
techniques.description: Using legitimate credentials — local, domain, cloud, or default — to access systems. Hard to detect because the activity rides authorised auth paths.

tactics.name: Execution
tactics.description: Running adversary-controlled code on a local or remote system. Almost every intrusion routes through some form of execution at some point.

techniques.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
techniques.description: Abusing a shell or scripting host (bash, PowerShell, cmd, Python) to run commands. Sub-techniques cover specific interpreters; T1059.004 is bash on Linux.

techniques.name: Native API
techniques.description: Calling OS-native functions directly (Win32 API, syscalls) instead of going through a higher-level interpreter — useful for evading command-line monitoring.

tactics.name: Persistence
tactics.description: Maintaining a foothold across reboots, credential rotations, and the user logging out. The adversary doesn't want to re-do initial access every time.

techniques.name: Create Account
techniques.description: Creating a new local, domain, or cloud account to keep access — typically a backdoor user that the adversary controls and the legitimate admin doesn't track.

techniques.name: Account Manipulation
techniques.description: Modifying an existing account (group membership, credentials, SSH keys, MFA tokens) to keep or extend access without creating a new one.

tactics.name: Privilege Escalation
tactics.description: Going from a low-privilege foothold (regular user) to higher rights (root, SYSTEM, domain admin) so the adversary can do things their current account can't.

techniques.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
techniques.description: Abusing a vulnerability in the kernel, driver, or privileged service to gain elevated rights — classic local-privesc exploit chain.

techniques.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
techniques.description: Bypassing legitimate elevation controls (sudo, UAC, setuid binaries) to run code with higher privileges than the calling process.

tactics.name: Defense Evasion
tactics.description: Avoiding being detected, blocked, or rolled back by defensive tooling. Spans disabling security agents, hiding artefacts, and masquerading as benign.

techniques.name: Masquerading
techniques.description: Making a malicious file or process look legitimate — by name (svch0st.exe), path, signing, or metadata — so users and tools mistake it for benign.

techniques.name: File and Directory Permissions Modification
techniques.description: Changing ACLs, ownership, or POSIX mode on files/directories to evade scanners or grant the adversary access they otherwise wouldn't have.

techniques.name: Impair Defenses
techniques.description: Disabling, modifying, or unloading security controls (AV, EDR, audit, firewall, logging) so the rest of the operation runs unobserved.

techniques.name: Indicator Removal on Host
techniques.description: Wiping evidence — clearing event logs, deleting bash history, removing dropped files — to slow incident response and hide the attack timeline.

techniques.name: Obfuscated Files or Information
techniques.description: Encoding, encrypting, packing, or otherwise obscuring code or data so static scanners and analysts can't easily understand what it does.

tactics.name: Credential Access
tactics.description: Stealing credentials — passwords, hashes, tokens, keys — to expand access or impersonate users. Strong overlap with Persistence and Lateral Movement.

techniques.name: Brute Force
techniques.description: Same technique as in Reconnaissance, but used against an internal authentication surface (SSH, SMB, AD) once the adversary is already inside.

tactics.name: Discovery
tactics.description: Mapping out the environment — what hosts exist, what software is running, what users are logged in, what's reachable. Almost every intrusion does this.

techniques.name: File and Directory Discovery
techniques.description: Listing files and folders to find configs, credentials, source code, or data of interest. ls -la, find, dir-style enumeration.

techniques.name: Process Discovery
techniques.description: Listing running processes (ps, tasklist) to understand what's on the host — defenders, dev tools, services worth targeting.

techniques.name: System Information Discovery
techniques.description: Reading host metadata — kernel/OS version, hostname, hardware, locale — to fingerprint the system and choose the right next move.

techniques.name: System Network Connections Discovery
techniques.description: Enumerating live TCP/UDP connections (netstat, ss) to map who's talking to whom and identify pivot targets or active sessions.

techniques.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
techniques.description: Reading network configuration — interfaces, routes, DNS, IP addresses (ifconfig, ip addr, route) — to understand reachability and segmentation.

techniques.name: System Owner/User Discovery
techniques.description: Finding out who owns the host or who's currently logged in (whoami, w, who) — crucial for picking the right credential to steal next.

techniques.name: Network Sniffing
techniques.description: Capturing network traffic on a host or segment to harvest credentials, tokens, or other sensitive data riding the wire.

tactics.name: Lateral Movement
tactics.description: Moving from the initial foothold to other systems in the network — pivoting toward the eventual objective. Often uses stolen credentials and built-in admin tools.

techniques.name: Remote Services
techniques.description: Using legitimate remote access protocols (SSH, RDP, SMB, WinRM) with valid (often stolen) credentials to log into other hosts in the network.

tactics.name: Collection
tactics.description: Gathering data of interest — files, screenshots, audio, keystrokes, mailboxes — and staging it locally before exfiltration.

techniques.name: Data from Local System
techniques.description: Reading files from the local filesystem of the compromised host — configs, source code, credentials, business documents — for later theft.

techniques.name: Network Sniffing
techniques.description: Same packet-capture technique listed under Discovery; in Collection the focus is harvesting payload data rather than mapping the network.

tactics.name: Command and Control
tactics.description: The channel the adversary uses to talk to compromised hosts — issue commands, deliver tools, exfil data. Designed to blend in with normal traffic.

techniques.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
techniques.description: Pulling additional tools or payloads from adversary infrastructure onto the victim host — wget/curl, scp, BITS, PowerShell DownloadFile.

techniques.name: Application Layer Protocol
techniques.description: Hiding C2 traffic inside common application protocols (HTTP/S, DNS, mail) so it looks like normal user activity to network monitoring.

tactics.name: Exfiltration
tactics.description: Stealing the data. Could be over the C2 channel, an alternate channel, or physical media — the goal is to get it out of the victim environment.

tactics.name: Impact
tactics.description: Disrupting, destroying, or manipulating the target — encrypting data for ransom, wiping disks, defacing services, denying access. The final "actions on objective".

techniques.name: Data Manipulation
techniques.description: Modifying data in place to influence business outcomes — falsifying records, tampering with stored data, altering data in transit.

techniques.name: Data Destruction
techniques.description: Permanently destroying data or systems to disrupt operations — overwriting files, wiping volumes, dropping tables. Recovery requires backups.
